## Libraries and data load

Libraries for data work and plotting, and for the models that follow.

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(parsnip)
library(rsample)
library(recipes)
library(workflows)
library(tune)
library(dials)
library(yardstick)
```

The response is `Democracy`, whether a country was a democracy in 2020. Every predictor is taken for 2020, the year of the democracy data.

```{r}
#| label: import
#| message: false
sanitation <- read_csv("../data/predictors/at_least_basic_sanitation_overall_access_percent.csv")
fertility  <- read_csv("../data/predictors/children_per_woman_total_fertility.csv")
co2        <- read_csv("../data/predictors/co2_pcap_cons.csv")
income     <- read_csv("../data/predictors/ilevels4_wb.csv", col_types = cols(.default = "c"))
poverty    <- read_csv("../data/predictors/number_of_people_in_poverty.csv")
democracy <- read_csv("../data/response/democracy2020.csv")
```

Clean data: drop the years after 2022 and change each file to long format, one row per country and year.

```{r}
#| label: drop-and-pivot
drop_and_pivot <- function(df, value_name) {
  df |>
    select(-any_of(as.character(2023:2100))) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = -c(geo, name),
      names_to = "year",
      values_to = value_name
    ) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year))
}

sanitation_long <- drop_and_pivot(sanitation, "sanitation_access_pct")
fertility_long  <- drop_and_pivot(fertility, "children_per_woman")
co2_long        <- drop_and_pivot(co2, "co2_per_capita")
income_long     <- drop_and_pivot(income, "income_level")
poverty_long    <- drop_and_pivot(poverty, "people_in_poverty")
```

Join variables into one data frame: keep 2020, add the response, and drop countries with any missing value.

```{r}
#| label: join
joined <- list(
  sanitation_long, fertility_long, co2_long,
  income_long, poverty_long
) |>
  reduce(full_join, by = c("geo", "name", "year")) |>
  filter(year == 2020) |>
  arrange(geo, year) |>
  inner_join(democracy, by = c("geo", "name"))

combined <- na.omit(joined)
write.csv(combined, "../data/combined_data.csv")
```

### Countries in the data

```{r}
#| label: missing-check
joined |>
  summarise(across(c(co2_per_capita, income_level, sanitation_access_pct,
                     people_in_poverty), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Missing values among countries with a democracy label")

joined |>
  count(Democracy, name = "all_countries") |>
  left_join(combined |> count(Democracy, name = "kept"), by = "Democracy") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Countries before and after dropping rows with missing values")

anti_join(joined, combined, by = "geo") |>
  select(name, Democracy, income_level, co2_per_capita) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Countries dropped for missing values")
```

The democracy file has 165 countries and 154 remain after dropping rows with a missing value. CO2 and income level are never the missing ones, since every dropped country lacks a sanitation or poverty value. Two high-CO2 non-democracies, Qatar and the UAE, are among the dropped countries, so all results below describe the 154 kept.

## Exploratory data analysis

Each predictor is graphed against the response, `Democracy`, and summarized by democracy group. Quantitative predictors get summary statistics and an outlier check, and the categorical income group gets a two way table.

## Variable 1: Children Per Woman

### Graph and description

```{r}
#| label: children-graph
combined |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = Democracy, y = children_per_woman)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Democracy vs Children Per Woman",
       x = "Democracy", y = "Children Per Woman") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Non-democratic countries generally have more children per woman, with a median of about 3.06 compared to 1.59 in democratic countries. Non-democratic countries also show greater variability.

### Stats and description

```{r}
#| label: children-stats
combined |>
  summarise(
    n_countries = n(),
    mean        = mean(children_per_woman),
    median      = median(children_per_woman),
    sd          = sd(children_per_woman),
    min         = min(children_per_woman),
    q1          = quantile(children_per_woman, 0.25),
    q3          = quantile(children_per_woman, 0.75),
    max         = max(children_per_woman),
    .by = Democracy
  )
```

1.  Non-democratic countries have a higher mean and median children per woman than democratic countries. They also have a larger standard deviation, indicating more variation. Six democracies are extreme outliers, led by Ghana at 3.54 children per woman, Namibia at 3.35 and Papua New Guinea at 3.27.

## Variable 2: CO2 Emissions Per Capita

`co2_per_capita` is quantitative and continuous, measured in tonnes of CO2 per person on a consumption basis. In 2020 the kept countries range from 0.02 to 24.1 tonnes, with no negative or missing values.

### Graph and description

```{r}
#| label: co2-graph
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6
ggplot(combined, aes(x = Democracy, y = co2_per_capita)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.6, color = "blue", size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5,
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Democracy vs CO2 Emissions per Capita, 2020",
       x = "Democracy", y = "CO2 per capita, tonnes",
       caption = "Each dot is a country. The black bar marks the group median.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Democratic countries emit more CO2 per person. Most non-democratic countries sit below 3 tonnes and half are below about 1 tonne, while democratic countries spread from about 0.4 to 24 tonnes. A few non-democracies reach far above the rest of their group.

### Stats and description

```{r}
#| label: co2-stats
combined |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarise(
    n_countries = n(),
    mean        = mean(co2_per_capita),
    median      = median(co2_per_capita),
    sd          = sd(co2_per_capita),
    min         = min(co2_per_capita),
    q1          = quantile(co2_per_capita, 0.25),
    q3          = quantile(co2_per_capita, 0.75),
    max         = max(co2_per_capita)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "CO2 per capita by democracy")
```

```{r}
#| label: co2-outliers
combined |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  filter(co2_per_capita > quantile(co2_per_capita, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR(co2_per_capita)) |>
  arrange(Democracy, desc(co2_per_capita)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Democracy, name, co2_per_capita) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Extreme CO2 outliers within each group")
```

```{r}
#| label: co2-overlap
co2_medians <- combined |>
  group_by(Democracy) |>
  summarise(m = median(co2_per_capita)) |>
  deframe()

tibble(
  statement = c("Democracies above the non-democratic median",
                "Non-democracies above the democratic median"),
  share = c(mean(combined$co2_per_capita[combined$Democracy == "Yes"] > co2_medians["No"]),
            mean(combined$co2_per_capita[combined$Democracy == "No"] > co2_medians["Yes"]))
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Overlap between the two groups")
```

Democratic countries have a mean of 6.18 and a median of 5.26 tonnes, against a mean of 2.63 and a median of 0.97 for non-democratic countries. The non-democratic mean is pulled up by a few heavy emitters, and the spread is similar in both groups, with standard deviations of 4.11 and 4.49. Among democracies 96% emit more than the non-democratic median, while only 14% of non-democracies emit more than the democratic median.

Ten non-democracies and one democracy are extreme outliers. The non-democratic ones are led by Kuwait at 22.1 tonnes, Saudi Arabia at 18.2 and Bahrain at 14.7, followed by Turkmenistan, Oman, Kazakhstan, Russia, Libya, Iran and China. Most are oil and gas exporters, and China and Russia are very large industrial economies. The one democratic outlier is Singapore at 24.1, a small wealthy trade hub. The lowest emitters are the DR Congo, Burundi and the Central African Republic, all non-democracies, and the lowest democracy is Timor-Leste at 0.42.

CO2 per capita is a useful predictor, since the middle halves of the two groups barely overlap, running from 0.37 to 2.65 tonnes for non-democracies and from 2.44 to 8.66 for democracies. Its main weakness is the group of oil and gas states, which are non-democratic but emit as much as rich democracies.

## Variable 3: Income Groups

`income_level` is categorical and ordinal with four levels: Low, Lower middle, Upper middle and High income, assigned by the World Bank from GNI per capita. It has no missing values among the kept countries, and it is ordered below so that plots and tables run from low to high.

```{r}
#| label: income-order
income_data <- combined |>
  mutate(income_level = factor(
    income_level,
    levels = c("Low income", "Lower middle income",
               "Upper middle income", "High income"),
    ordered = TRUE
  ))
```

### Graph and description

```{r}
#| label: income-graph
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6
ggplot(income_data, aes(x = income_level, fill = Democracy)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(No = "orange", Yes = "blue")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Democracy by World Bank Income Group, 2020",
       x = "Income group", y = "Share of countries", fill = "Democracy") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The share of democracies rises steadily with income. No low income country is a democracy, about a quarter of lower middle income countries are, about half of upper middle income countries are, and nearly all high income countries are.

### Two way table and description

```{r}
#| label: income-tables
income_table <- table(income_data$income_level, income_data$Democracy)

knitr::kable(addmargins(income_table),
             caption = "Number of countries by income group and democracy")

knitr::kable(round(prop.table(income_table, margin = 1), 3),
             caption = "Share of each income group that is democratic or not")

knitr::kable(round(prop.table(income_table, margin = 2), 3),
             caption = "Share of each democracy group in each income level")
```

Of the 154 countries, 45% are democracies. The share is 0% of 24 low income countries, 23% of 48 lower middle income countries, 54% of 41 upper middle income countries and 90% of 41 high income countries. Looking the other way, 53% of the 70 democracies are high income and none are low income, while 44% of the 84 non-democracies are lower middle income, 29% are low income and only 5% are high income.

The four high income non-democracies are Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman and Saudi Arabia, all Gulf oil exporters. Qatar and the UAE, dropped above for a missing poverty value, fit the same pattern.

```{r}
#| label: income-co2
income_data |>
  group_by(income_level) |>
  summarise(n_countries = n(), median_co2 = median(co2_per_capita),
            mean_co2 = mean(co2_per_capita)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "CO2 per capita by income group")
```

CO2 per capita rises with income, from a median of 0.19 tonnes for low income countries to 8.67 for high income countries. The two predictors therefore capture overlapping information.

## Which variable for single variable models?

Each predictor is scored with two rough measures. Accuracy is the share of countries classified correctly by the best single cutoff on that predictor. AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen democracy scores higher than a randomly chosen non-democracy on the predictor, taken in whichever direction is stronger. A value of 0.5 means no separation and 1 means perfect separation.

```{r}
#| label: predictor-comparison
is_democracy <- combined$Democracy == "Yes"

rank_auc <- function(x, y) {
  r <- rank(x)
  n_yes <- sum(y)
  n_no <- sum(!y)
  auc <- (sum(r[y]) - n_yes * (n_yes + 1) / 2) / (n_yes * n_no)
  max(auc, 1 - auc)
}

best_cutoff_accuracy <- function(x, y) {
  cutoffs <- sort(unique(x))
  max(map_dbl(cutoffs, \(t) max(mean((x > t) == y), mean((x <= t) == y))))
}

income_rank <- match(
  combined$income_level,
  c("Low income", "Lower middle income", "Upper middle income", "High income")
)

predictors <- list(
  "Children per woman"       = combined$children_per_woman,
  "CO2 emissions per capita" = combined$co2_per_capita,
  "Income group"             = income_rank,
  "Basic sanitation access"  = combined$sanitation_access_pct,
  "People in poverty"        = combined$people_in_poverty
)

tibble(
  predictor = names(predictors),
  accuracy  = map_dbl(predictors, best_cutoff_accuracy, y = is_democracy),
  auc       = map_dbl(predictors, rank_auc, y = is_democracy)
) |>
  arrange(desc(auc)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Single predictor strength for separating democracies")
```

```{r}
#| label: predictor-correlations
combined |>
  select(children_per_woman, co2_per_capita, sanitation_access_pct, people_in_poverty) |>
  cor() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Correlations between the quantitative predictors")
```

Income group and children per woman are nearly tied as the strongest predictors, with AUCs of about 0.86 each, and CO2 comes next at 0.81. Sanitation and poverty are the weakest. We suggest children per woman for the single variable models, because it has the best accuracy at 79% and is quantitative with many distinct values, which suits both kNN distances and a logistic curve. Income group has only four distinct values, which makes it awkward for kNN. Children per woman and sanitation are strongly related, with a correlation of -0.85, so the all variable models will carry some duplicated information. These are rough checks on the same data used to build them, and cross validation in the models will test them properly.

## kNN classification

### Single variable model

Make a kNN model using your best predictor variable

```{r}
#| label: recipe_creation
knn_single_variable_recipe <- recipe(Democracy~income_level, data = combined) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

knn_all_variable_recipe <- recipe(Democracy~income_level+sanitation_access_pct+children_per_woman+co2_per_capita+people_in_poverty, data = combined) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())|>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```

#### Model tuning to find k

```{r}
#| label: model-tuning-k-single-variable
set.seed(1776)
val_split <- validation_split(combined, prop = 0.8)

knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors=tune(),  weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

knn_wf_single<-workflow()|>
  add_recipe(knn_single_variable_recipe)|>
  add_model(knn_spec)

knn_grid <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from=3, to=21, by=2)) 
class_met=metric_set(accuracy)
knn_cv <- tune_grid(
  knn_wf_single,
  resamples = val_split,
  grid = knn_grid
)
cv_metrics_knn<-collect_metrics(knn_cv)
cv_metrics_knn

autoplot(knn_cv, metric = "accuracy")
best_k <- select_best(knn_cv, metric = "accuracy")
best_k
```

#### Model for best k

```{r}
#| label: best-single-variable-model
knn_spec<-nearest_neighbor(neighbors=3,  weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

knn_wf_single<-workflow()|>
  add_recipe(knn_single_variable_recipe)|>
  add_model(knn_spec)

single_knn_model <- 
  knn_wf_single |> 
  fit(data = combined)
```

#### Model evaluation-accuracy, cv for overfitting

```{r}
#| label: single-variable-model-evaluation
set.seed(1776)
folds <- vfold_cv(combined, v = 10)

knn_cv_single <- tune_grid(
  knn_wf_single,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = knn_grid,
  metrics = class_met
)

best_k_single <- select_best(knn_cv_single, metric = "accuracy")
collect_metrics(knn_cv_single)
```

There is not clear evidence of overfitting when comparing against the accuracy of the cross-validation model. The accuracy scores on both models are roughly the same, which leans towards the model not overfitting.

### All variable model

Make a kNN model using all your predictor variables

#### Model tuning to find k using cv.

```{r}
#| label: model-tuning-k-all-variables
set.seed(1776)
val_split <- validation_split(combined, prop = 0.8)

knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors=tune(),  weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

knn_wf_all<-workflow()|>
  add_recipe(knn_all_variable_recipe)|>
  add_model(knn_spec)

knn_grid <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from=3, to=21, by=2)) 
class_met=metric_set(accuracy)
knn_cv <- tune_grid(
  knn_wf_all,
  resamples = val_split,
  grid = knn_grid
)
cv_metrics_knn<-collect_metrics(knn_cv)
cv_metrics_knn

autoplot(knn_cv, metric = "accuracy")
best_k <- select_best(knn_cv, metric = "accuracy")
best_k
```

#### Model for best k

```{r}
#| label: best-all-variables-model
knn_spec<-nearest_neighbor(neighbors=5,  weight_func = "rectangular") |>
  set_engine("kknn")|>
  set_mode("classification")

knn_wf_all<-workflow()|>
  add_recipe(knn_all_variable_recipe)|>
  add_model(knn_spec)

all_knn_model <- 
  knn_wf_all |> 
  fit(data = combined)
```

#### Model evaluation-accuracy, cv for overfitting

```{r}
#| label: all-variables-model-evaluation
set.seed(1776)
folds <- vfold_cv(combined, v = 10)

knn_cv_all <- tune_grid(
  knn_wf_all,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = knn_grid,
  metrics = class_met
)

best_k_all <- select_best(knn_cv_all, metric = "accuracy")
collect_metrics(knn_cv_all)
```

There is no noticeable gap between the cross-validation model mean accuracy and the accuracy in the best model. The difference between the mean accuracy and accuracy of the best model seems to be roughly the same as the single variable model. I would say there is no overfitting present in this model.

### Which model was best?

Of the two kNN models, the best performing one was the multivariate model. It had the higher accuracy when finding the best k as well as during cross-validation. I would say the trade off of complexity was not worth it as we only gained a small increase to accuracy at the cost of adding four addition variables. This will make the model harder to interpret.

## Your question

Is access to basic sanitation associated with the average number of children per woman across countries?

### Discussion

Access to basic sanitation is an important indicator of living conditions and public health. We wanted to investigate whether countries with greater access to basic sanitation tend to have lower fertility rates. Comparing these two variables may help us understand how different aspects of development are associated across countries.

```{r}
combined |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sanitation_access_pct, y = children_per_woman)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Sanitation Access vs. Children per Woman",
    x = "Access to Basic Sanitation (%)",
    y = "Children per Woman",
    caption = "Each point represents a country in 2020."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
combined |>
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(sanitation_access_pct, children_per_woman)
  )
```

### Answer

The visualization shows a strong negative relationship between access to basic sanitation and the number of children per woman. Countries with higher access to basic sanitation generally have fewer children per woman, while countries with lower sanitation access tend to have higher fertility rates. The correlation coefficient of -0.846 supports this observation, indicating a strong negative association between the two variables. However, this relationship does not establish causation, and other factors, such as income, education, and healthcare access, may also contribute to the observed pattern.
